title: RE-TRAC: REcursive TRAjectory Compression for Deep Search Agents
one_liner: Keep a search agent from wandering by making each round leave behind a compact state that the next round must read before acting.
lead: A deep-search agent rarely fails because it cannot do one search. It fails because after several searches it forgets what it already learned, repeats weak branches, or keeps pushing down a path that is no longer promising. Re-TRAC changes the unit of progress. Instead of treating each trajectory as a self-contained attempt, it turns every completed trajectory into a structured state that records evidence, open questions, failed ideas, and next-step plans. Later trajectories start from that compressed state, so the agent can revisit, branch, and refine with a view of the whole search rather than only the latest local context.

problem.h2: Why linear search trajectories get trapped
paras: A ReAct-style agent usually works in a straight line. It asks a question, issues a tool call, reads the result, and decides the next move from the running conversation. That is workable for short tasks, but deep research is not a short task. By the time the agent has explored several branches, the earlier evidence is buried in long context and the current decision is driven mostly by whatever was seen most recently.

That design creates three linked failures. The agent struggles to return to a promising earlier branch because the earlier branch is no longer represented in a compact form. It struggles to compare alternative branches because each one lives inside a different long trace. And it struggles to stop redundant exploration because the system does not hold a global summary of what is already known. Re-TRAC addresses all three by turning every finished trajectory into an explicit search state.

callout.html: Replace a purely linear search history with a compressed state after each trajectory so later trajectories can plan with global memory instead of only local recency.

steps.text: Let the agent search, read sources, and produce an intermediate result for one branch.
Write a structured state that lists accepted evidence, unresolved questions, failed directions, and concrete next plans.

steps.b: Condition the next trajectory on that state
steps.text: Start the next search round from the compressed state so the agent uses the global summary when choosing actions.
Allow later rounds to revisit earlier branches, test alternatives, and merge evidence from multiple paths because each round starts from a state that records what every earlier path found.
Keep updating the state until the evidence is strong enough to support a final answer.

paras: The paper changes the representation of search progress. Instead of storing progress only as a long action trace, it creates a structured state between trajectories and uses that state as the object carried forward.
object.object: the carried-forward state between search trajectories

hidden.name: global search coverage
paras: The real question is not how many tool calls the agent made. The real question is how much of the search space the agent has already covered in a usable form. A search process can make many calls and still have poor coverage because its results are scattered across traces that cannot be compared or reused easily.

Re-TRAC raises usable coverage by compressing each trajectory into a state that later rounds can read directly. That matters because a compact state preserves what was learned, marks what is still missing, and records which branches already failed, so later work spends more effort on uncovered areas.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark parts of the search state that help later trajectories avoid repeating old work.

reads.html: The method tries to keep a reusable map of what the agent has already checked and what still needs work.
Cross-trajectory reflection improves search because later trajectories are conditioned on a state that summarizes evidence, uncertainty, failure cases, and future plans.

paras: The method works because it separates two jobs that are often mixed together in one long conversation. One job is exploring a branch: opening sources, checking facts, and seeing whether a lead holds up. The other job is carrying forward the durable result of that exploration. When those jobs are mixed, the agent has to recover the durable result from a noisy trace every time it starts a new step.

Re-TRAC makes the durable result explicit. After each trajectory, it writes down which evidence is accepted, which uncertainties remain, which branches failed, and what should be tried next. That improves later trajectories because they no longer need to infer the search state from a pile of messages. The paper also reports fewer tool calls and lower context use across rounds, which makes sense because the state narrows later exploration to unanswered questions instead of revisiting the same branches.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Start with State_1 containing only the question and two open questions.
Round 1 checks one source and finds one reliable fact, one failed branch, and one unresolved gap.
Compress(State_1, Trajectory_1) writes those into State_2.
Round 2 reads State_2, skips the failed branch, and directly targets the unresolved gap.
That saves work because the next trajectory starts from the search summary rather than rebuilding it from the full earlier trace.

math.note: The paper's exact state format is richer, but the recurrence captures the main idea: each trajectory is turned into a smaller state that guides the next one.

charts.title: Plain linear search
charts.note: Linear search loses global awareness because each new move leans too heavily on the recent trace.

charts.title: Re-TRAC
charts.note: The structured state keeps later rounds focused because the agent can see what was settled, what failed, and what still needs evidence.

items.b: Compression can throw away a useful detail.
items.html: If the state is too short, later trajectories may miss a source detail that mattered, because the durable summary was incomplete.

items.b: A wrong state can mislead every later round.
items.html: If the state records a weak claim as settled fact, the next trajectories inherit that mistake because they are conditioned on the state.
If the planner keeps opening new branches without closing old uncertainties, search can stay broad but unproductive because the state keeps expanding faster than evidence is resolved.
The state should keep verified evidence separate from open questions and failed leads so later trajectories know what can be trusted and what still needs checking.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small research agent over a multi-hop question set. Let one version use a plain linear trace. Let the second version end every trajectory by writing four fields: accepted evidence, unresolved questions, failed branches, and next plans. Feed those four fields into the next trajectory.

Measure answer quality, number of repeated searches, and how many later rounds introduce new evidence. The demo should show that the state-guided system wastes fewer rounds because each new trajectory starts from a compact summary of the whole search.
demo.closing: If reuse_gain is clearly above 1, the state is helping later trajectories build on earlier work instead of replaying it.
